ai.definition: Space Travel Milestones refer to significant achievements in human spaceflight technology aimed at expanding human presence beyond Earth, including missions to the Moon, Mars, and asteroids.
ai.howItWorks: These milestones are achieved through advancements in rocket propulsion technologies (reusability), life support systems, and mission planning techniques. Reusable rockets reduce costs by allowing launch vehicles to return to Earth intact for refurbishment and reuse, while advanced life support systems enable longer-duration space missions with minimal resupply.
ai.problemSolved: Historical limitations of single-use rockets, high operational costs, and the need for sustainable long-term human habitation in space.
ai.manufacturing: Manufacturing involves developing and testing new rocket designs, integrating advanced materials, and creating robust life support systems. This process requires significant investment in R&D infrastructure and specialized equipment.
ai.buildProcess: The build process includes design iteration, component fabrication, assembly, and rigorous testing to ensure safety and reliability before launch.
ai.costDrivers: Cost drivers include the development of reusable rocket technologies, advanced materials for spacecraft construction, and life support system innovations. Manufacturing costs are high due to specialized equipment and labor-intensive processes.
ai.lifecycleOutlook: The outlook is positive with increasing private investment and government support, but challenges remain in scaling production and reducing overall mission costs.
ai.regulation: Regulatory frameworks vary by country, focusing on safety standards, environmental impact assessments, and international cooperation agreements. There are ongoing efforts to harmonize regulations across jurisdictions.
ai.risks: Technical risks include rocket failures during launch or re-entry, life support system malfunctions, and potential health issues for astronauts due to microgravity environments. Economic risks involve high upfront costs and uncertain return on investment.
ai.profitability: Profitability is challenging in the short term but could improve with successful mission execution and commercialization of space resources such as minerals from asteroids or tourism services.
ai.futureDevelopment: Future developments may include further miniaturization of electronics, more efficient propulsion systems, and enhanced life support technologies to extend human presence in space. There is also potential for increased collaboration between private companies and governments.
ai.energyRequirements: Field units draw low hundreds of watts; fabrication is energy-intensive due to vacuum baking and high-temperature processes.

glossary.def: Rocket systems designed for multiple launches after refurbishment, significantly reducing operational costs.
Integrated equipment and processes providing essential services like air, water, food, and waste management for astronauts in space.
The establishment of permanent human settlements on celestial bodies such as the Moon or Mars.
Extracting valuable resources from asteroids using advanced robotic technologies and transporting them back to Earth or other locations for processing and use.

subsystems.name: Launch and re-entry
subsystems.role: gets mass off Earth cheaply and brings crews back safely.

subsystems.name: In-space propulsion and transfer
subsystems.role: moves payloads between orbits and towards other worlds.

subsystems.name: Habitat and life support
subsystems.role: keeps a crew alive in a sealed volume for years.

subsystems.name: Power
subsystems.role: supplies electricity far from the Sun.
parts: fission surface reactors (demonstrated on the ground only)

subsystems.name: Crew health and radiation protection
subsystems.role: limits bone loss, muscle loss and radiation damage.

subsystems.name: Surface systems and resource use
subsystems.role: makes air, water and propellant from local material instead of hauling it.
parts: electrolysis of water into oxygen and hydrogen

subsystems.name: Communications and navigation
subsystems.role: tracks and commands spacecraft across interplanetary distances.

buildSteps.title: Reach low Earth orbit
buildSteps.detail: A reusable launcher places crew and cargo in orbit; routine reuse is what makes the rest affordable.

buildSteps.title: Refuel in orbit
buildSteps.detail: Propellant is transferred between tanks in microgravity so a vehicle can leave Earth's vicinity with a full load.

buildSteps.title: Cruise to the destination
buildSteps.detail: Months of coasting on a minimum-energy trajectory, with the crew protected from radiation and kept healthy by closed-loop life support.

buildSteps.title: Land on the surface
buildSteps.detail: Aerodynamic entry, a heat shield, parachutes and retro-rockets slow the vehicle in an atmosphere thinner than Earth's.

buildSteps.title: Set up the outpost
buildSteps.detail: Habitats, power and drilling equipment are deployed; local ice is processed into water, oxygen and rocket propellant.

buildSteps.title: Live and work
buildSteps.detail: Crews run science, maintain equipment and prove that a settlement can survive a full seasonal cycle.

buildSteps.title: Return
buildSteps.detail: A pre-positioned ascent vehicle lifts the crew back to orbit and a transfer stage brings them home.

prerequisites.why: reusable first stages fly routinely, but full reusability at very large scale is still being proven.
small-scale transfers have been flown; the large cryogenic transfers a Mars mission needs have not.
orbital stations recycle most air and water, but not food, and need steady resupply.
no flown design keeps crews below accepted dose limits on a multi-year interplanetary trip.
making oxygen from Martian air was demonstrated by a small instrument on a rover, but at gram scale.
sample return from asteroids has been done; mining and processing ore in space has not.

pathway.milestone: commercial crews and cargo flying to low Earth orbit in reusable vehicles
pathway.unlocks: cheap, frequent access to space and experience with long-duration crews.

pathway.milestone: a sustained lunar surface programme with habitats, rovers and ice prospecting
pathway.unlocks: practice at living off local resources beyond Earth orbit.

pathway.milestone: orbital propellant depots and robotic Mars sample return
pathway.unlocks: the transport architecture and planetary-protection rules a crewed Mars trip depends on.

pathway.milestone: crewed Mars surface missions and, much later, industrial use of asteroid material
pathway.unlocks: a permanent human presence off Earth and off-world supply chains.
